extracted.intended_audience: newspaper reporters and journalism students (particularly city/local reporters and those learning interview technique)
extracted.subtask_description: Preparing for, conducting, and writing up interviews for newspaper stories: planning questions, managing interview dynamics, eliciting usable material, and structuring the resulting interview story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write out the questions / prepare in advance
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare a list of questions before the interview rather than relying on ad libbing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reporter is the ringmaster; without a plan he is likely to get no more than he could from a two-minute telephone call. Memorize a series of queries to draw upon by rote in case of nervousness or fast-talking interviewees. Preparing in advance helps avoid faltering, wasted time, and falling into the mire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporter as ringmaster / direct the interview
rubrics_metrics.description: The reporter must direct the interview, steering it away from unproductive discussion toward printable aspects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not count on ad-libbed questions. Like an architect with a detailed plan, the reporter must know precisely what should be done and keep control so the interview yields usable material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare for and manage stage fright
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that stage fright can sap self-confidence; preparation and memorized questions prevent freezing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A touch of stage fright early may be helpful, but it should not persist. Memorized questions let the reporter survive the minutes until self-possession returns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle taciturn or monosyllabic interviewees
rubrics_metrics.description: Use planned direction and unity to extract usable material even from interviewees who reply curtly with 'Yes' or 'No.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the interviewee will not volunteer information, a thought-out plan of attack allows one-word replies to form a foundation for a fair story; use 'ticklers' or baiting questions to get longer replies.

rubrics_metrics.name: The vital first minute — introduce yourself and state purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: In the first sixty seconds, introduce yourself formally as a reporter and make your purpose clear to avoid later misunderstandings or refusals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not apologize or belittle yourself. State that you are there because the interviewee can speak authoritatively on a subject of interest to many readers. How you meet the initial response often determines whether the interview is productive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responding to hostile or resistant opening reactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize six common hostile responses and handle each with a practiced reply or tactic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The six types and suggested handling: (1) 'I don't like your paper' — don't argue; let criticism bounce off ('We try to make it a good paper'); (2) 'I've always been misquoted' — sympathize briefly then assure verification ('Before I leave I'll verify everything you say'); (3) 'Why do you come to me? I'm not news' — reply that your job is to know who speaks as an expert; (4) the egoist who insults — usually ignore the discourtesy and proceed; deflation can work only rarely; (5) 'I'm too busy' — promise brevity ('I'll be brief — take only a moment or two'); once talking begins it may continue; (6) 'No statement until next week' — size up motive (news unripe, show-off, or grudge-holder) and respond by agreeing, arranging return, or explaining the paper's needs; probing the reason can defuse a grudge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Go to headquarters / seek authoritative sources
rubrics_metrics.description: For policy or authoritative statements, interview the person with decision-making authority rather than subordinates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subordinates often protect themselves by feigning ignorance; an executive or officer can speak with authority. If necessary, gather preliminary information from underlings under pledge that it won't be printed until you have the executive's consent, so the executive may be more willing to speak.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use preliminary information/off-the-record tactically
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtain background or off-the-record details from subordinates to prepare for the executive interview, but protect sources and manage disclosure carefully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the reporter already knows the information, an executive who might otherwise kill the interview may be willing to speak to ensure accuracy. Promise not to attribute subordinate comments and don't reveal who supplied off-the-record material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nut-cracking devices to elicit speech (use with caution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two techniques to get a silent interviewee to talk: state an outrageous distortion to provoke correction, or wait them out in silence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example of false assertion: state something blatantly incorrect so the subject corrects and then continues. The silence/wait-out is dangerous and akin to poker — success depends on acting ability and risk; do not experiment with it on important interviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure the interview into blocks/steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide the interview into phases (blocks) such as introduction, getting the interviewee talking, expanding to other topics, and verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical blocks: Block 1 — introduce and establish friendly rapport (use name, eye contact); Block 2 — get the subject talking (use ticklers or broad questions); Block 3 — adjust questions to draw out interesting points and broaden scope; Block 4 — verification of names, dates, facts and protection against misquotation. Judge pacing and combine blocks as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification at the end / protect against misquotation
rubrics_metrics.description: Reserve a final phase to check and re-state the facts and key remarks you plan to use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask again about names, dates, and facts; compel the interviewee to correct or modify statements now so they cannot later complain of misquotation. This protects the reporter and improves accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Note-taking vs memory — adapt to interviewee comfort
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide early whether to take notes or rely on memory based on the interviewee's reaction to written notes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early in the interview ask 'Do you mind if I write down that remark of yours?' If willingness or relief is shown, keep paper visible; if shyness arises, put paper away and rely on memory, then record immediately after leaving. Some are reassured by notes; others become timid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letting tangents vs steering the interview
rubrics_metrics.description: Be alert to tangents and decide how far to allow digressions — some are worthless, others lead to better stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a tangent yields richer material than the planned line, follow it; otherwise bring the interview back to useful topics. The reporter must judge value as the interview proceeds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brighten the story by restoring the human element
rubrics_metrics.description: Include description of appearance, actions, and the 'way in which he said it' to give personality to the interview story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During lean times interviews were clipped to 'what he said' with personality removed. Today there is room to restore human detail — narration, description, and conversation — rather than turning the piece into a monotonous Q&A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead must identify the interviewee and include the news peg
rubrics_metrics.description: Put the interview's news identification high in the lead so readers understand why this person's views matter and, when applicable, tie the interview to the relevant news event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid blind leads (e.g., a quote without who or why). Example: include that Mr. Nygard 'returned last week after a five-month tour through Sweden' to justify his comment on Swedish politics. For interviews related to prior news, insert the news peg prominently so readers see the connection (example: linking hospital emergency systems to a recent power failure elsewhere).

rubrics_metrics.name: Vary structure; avoid dull question-and-answer format
rubrics_metrics.description: Use varied sentence structures and speech-story lead devices to prevent monotony; don't reduce interviews to a series of 'Do you…?' 'No' answers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When replies are blunt 'Yes' or 'No', combine the question and answer into a single sentence (example given about city tax rate) rather than repeated Q&A. Use speech-story lead devices and fresh, original writing to keep interviews lively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics when interviewee refuses to answer
rubrics_metrics.description: Respect refusals on thoroughly private matters but, for topics of public import, report refusal fairly by giving both the question and the refusal to answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the subject is purely private, do not lampoon or force the issue. If the topic is of public import, present the refusal and the question to inform readers of the subject's non-cooperation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid interviewing yourself / asking slanted questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not try to entice the interviewee to express the reporter's viewpoint with leading or slanted questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the reporter becomes a sounding board for his own slanted questions, the interviewee will lose interest and the interview will fail. Ask neutral, open questions to elicit the subject's views.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be a good listener — show interest and maintain the 'happy medium' in attention
rubrics_metrics.description: Active, eager listening encourages fuller answers, reduces misquoting, and helps the reporter control the interview; avoid extremes of listlessness or breathless expectancy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A yawny, ceiling-gazing reporter kills loquacity. Listening forces the reporter to follow closely, lowering misunderstanding. But do not stare obsessively — look directly without making the subject uncomfortable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporter demeanor — natural, informal dignity; do not apologize
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct yourself with calm confidence; do not belittle or apologize, as that signals the interview is unimportant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present yourself as the person who has come because the interviewee can speak authoritatively to many readers. Apologizing implies the topic is inconsequential and may reduce the interviewee's willingness to engage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure and composition of the interview story
rubrics_metrics.description: Write the interview story using blocks: lead with the news peg, a secondary lead summarizing main comments, a catch‑foil or context paragraph, elaboration with quoted material, and amplification of secondary points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The same structure used for speech stories applies. The specimen layout shows: First block (lead with news peg), Second block (secondary lead), Third block (catch‑oil/context), Fourth block (elaboration with combined Q&A where appropriate), Fifth block (amplification). Use direct quotes judiciously and combine Q&A when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interview forms and source selection (folo, person interviews)
rubrics_metrics.description: Know the different interview forms — the 'folo' (local follow), interviews based on a particular person (opinion interviews), and feature interviews — and choose subjects appropriate to each form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Folos convert regional or national items into local angles (ask how a change affects the city). Person interviews can be opinion interviews tied to news or feature interviews with slight news peg; select people who are well informed on the topic and avoid repeating the same few sources too often.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overusing the same sources; match interviewee to topic expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultivate a variety of interview sources and restrict interviewees to subjects they are actually informed about.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If 'the same two or three' are used repeatedly, readers tire. Do not ask, for instance, a clergyman about specialist topics (e.g., Iceland weather) outside his expertise. Seek new interview sources and match topics to people's real knowledge.
